title: Liu, P. J., Rim, S., Min, L., & Min, K. E. (2023). The surprise of reaching out: Appreciated more than we think. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 124(4), 754-771.
status: used: Across preregistered experiments, people who reached out to someone in their social circle underestimated how much the recipient appreciated it.
notes: Abstract-level finding only; no effect sizes are shown.

title: Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2018). Undervaluing gratitude: Expressers misunderstand the consequences of showing appreciation. Psychological Science, 29(9).
status: used: People who wrote gratitude letters underestimated how surprised and positive recipients would feel, and overestimated how awkward recipients would feel.

title: Boothby, E. J., & Bohns, V. K. (2021). Why a simple act of kindness is not as simple as it seems: Underestimating the positive impact of our compliments on others. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 47(5), 826-840.
status: used: Compliment givers underestimated how positively recipients would feel and overestimated how bothered and uncomfortable they would be.

title: Epley, N., & Schroeder, J. (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980-1999.
status: used: Train and bus commuters told to talk with a stranger reported a more positive, and no less productive, commute than those told to sit in solitude; separate participants predicted the opposite.

title: Kardas, M., Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2022). Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 122(3), 367-398.
status: used: Deep conversations between strangers felt less awkward and created more connection and happiness than participants expected.

title: Levitt, S. D. (2021). Heads or tails: The impact of a coin toss on major life decisions and subsequent happiness. Review of Economic Studies, 88(1), 378-405.
status: used: Undecided people told by a coin toss to make an important change (e.g. quit a job, end a relationship) were more likely to make it, and those who changed reported being happier two and six months later. Participants were self-selected.

title: Gilbert, D. T., & Ebert, J. E. J. (2002). Decisions and revisions: The affective forecasting of changeable outcomes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 82(4), 503-514.
status: used: People preferred decisions they could change, but those who could change their minds liked their outcome less than those who could not. Reversibility is cheap to exercise, not free.

title: Gilovich, T., & Medvec, V. H. (1995). The experience of regret: What, when, and why. Psychological Review, 102(2), 379-395.
status: used: Regrets of action dominate in the short term; regrets of inaction dominate in the long term.

title: Richardson, J., & Gilovich, T. (2023). A very public replication of the temporal pattern to people's regrets.
status: used: Replicated the interaction between action/inaction and time perspective, though the exact pattern differed from the original.

title: Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2011). Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667-683.
status: used: Unfulfilled goals produced intrusive thoughts and interference on unrelated tasks; writing a specific plan removed those effects without completing the goal.

title: Killingsworth, M. A., & Gilbert, D. T. (2010). A wandering mind is an unhappy mind. Science, 330(6006), 932.
status: used: Among 2,250 adults sampled by smartphone, minds wandered in 46.9% of samples, and people were less happy when their minds wandered.

title: Mark, G., Gudith, D., & Klocke, U. (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. Proceedings of CHI 2008, 107-110.
status: used: Interrupted people finished tasks faster with no loss of quality, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort.
